content: Glucose-6-phosphate, also referred to as Robison ester, is a glucose molecule that has been phosphorylated at the sixth carbon position. This compound is highly prevalent in cells because the majority of glucose entering a cell undergoes phosphorylation in this manner. Due to its central role in cellular metabolism, glucose-6-phosphate can follow several metabolic pathways within the cell. Glucose-6-phosphate is a key intermediate at the beginning of two major metabolic pathways: glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway. Additionally, it can be converted into glycogen or starch for storage. In multicellular animals, glucose is stored as glycogen in the liver and muscles, while in other organisms, it is stored as intracellular starch or glycogen granules. Production of Glucose-6-Phosphate From Glucose Within cells, glucose-6-phosphate is generated by the phosphorylation of glucose at the sixth carbon. This reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme hexokinase in most cells, and by glucokinase in certain cells, particularly liver cells, in higher animals. This process consumes one molecule of ATP. The primary purpose of phosphorylating glucose immediately upon entry into the cell is to prevent it from diffusing back out. The addition of a charged phosphate group ensures that glucose-6-phosphate cannot easily cross the cell membrane. From Glycogen Glucose-6-phosphate is also produced during glycogenolysis, where glycogen is broken down into glucose-1-phosphate, which is then converted into glucose-6-phosphate. Fate 1: Pentose Phosphate Pathway When the ratio of NADP+ to NADPH increases, the cell recognizes the need to produce more NADPH, a reducing agent required for processes such as fatty acid synthesis and glutathione reduction in erythrocytes. In this case, glucose-6-phosphate is dehydrogenated by the enzyme glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase. This reaction, which is reversible, is the first step of the pentose phosphate pathway. This pathway generates NADPH and ribulose-5-phosphate, a precursor for the synthesis of other molecules. Additionally, if the cell requires nucleotide precursors for DNA synthesis and growth, glucose-6-phosphate will also enter the pentose phosphate pathway. Fate 2: Glycolysis If the cell requires energy or carbon skeletons for biosynthesis, glucose-6-phosphate is directed toward glycolysis. The first step in this pathway involves the isomerization of glucose-6-phosphate into fructose-6-phosphate by the enzyme phosphoglucose isomerase. This reaction prepares the molecule for further phosphorylation into fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. The addition of the second phosphate group is an irreversible step, committing glucose-6-phosphate to glycolysis for ATP production. Fate 3: Storage as Glycogen When blood glucose levels are high, the body stores excess glucose as glycogen. After being converted to glucose-6-phosphate, the enzyme phosphoglucomutase converts it into glucose-1-phosphate. Glucose-1-phosphate is then combined with uridine triphosphate (UTP) to form UDP-glucose, a reaction driven by the hydrolysis of pyrophosphate. The activated UDP-glucose is added to a growing glycogen molecule by glycogen synthase. This storage mechanism is highly efficient, requiring only one ATP molecule to store one glucose molecule and minimal energy to retrieve it. Glucose-6-phosphate also acts as an allosteric activator of glycogen synthase, ensuring that excess glucose is stored as glycogen when glucose levels are high. Conversely, glycogen synthase is inhibited when phosphorylated by protein kinase during times of stress or low blood glucose levels, as induced by hormones like glucagon or adrenaline. When glucose is needed for energy, glycogen phosphorylase cleaves glucose molecules from glycogen chains, producing glucose-1-phosphate, which is then converted back into glucose-6-phosphate by phosphoglucomutase. The phosphate group on glucose-6-phosphate can be removed by glucose-6-phosphatase, forming free glucose that can enter the bloodstream. Fate 4: Dephosphorylation and Release into the Bloodstream Liver cells contain the enzyme glucose-6-phosphatase, which removes the phosphate group from glucose-6-phosphate produced during glycogenolysis or gluconeogenesis. The resulting free glucose is released into the bloodstream, where it can be taken up by other cells in the body.
